posts.author: Hans
posts.content_md:
Yesterday Kris Meerlo and I had a chance to cross sensitize the excellent HF53 film from Filmotec. This film is normally sensitive only to green light. Using this method (originally invented by DannyB), the film gets an equal sensitivity to 633nm as it already has to the 532nm.

The method uses a solution that was invented by Jeff Blyth for the diffusion method. Here is the procedure:

STOCK DYE SOLUTION:

- 1 gram Pinacyanol Chloride in 100ml methanol.

SENSITIZATION SOLUTION:

- 66ml Methanol + 33ml de-ionized Water + 2.5ml Stock Dye Solution

PROCEDURE:

- Dip the film for one minute in the Sensitization Solution and wash in de-ionized water for one minute.

- Optionally the film can be made more sensitive by immersing in a solution of Ascorbic acid (1%) made to PH5.0 with Sodium Carbonate.

For developing a solution of Pyrogallol + Sodium Carbonate works really well with this film.

Hey Hans ! I certainly did not "invent" that use of pinacyanol chloride (or quinaldine Blue) in methanol. That was done around the 1850 's by photographic pioneers as well as being used by Lippmann and Neuhaus and others .

On the matter of using additional sensitizing effects with ascorbic acid at "pH 5.0" I now find that I can take it higher still to pH 7-to 8 to get still more sensitivity. I originally settled on pH 5. because when I put the film away after it had been sensitized with pH higher than 5 , I got some fogging trouble later. But now I don't get that trouble. It is probable that this issue needs to be "trial and error-ed" for each individual make of film or plate.

Now I want to whisper something in your ear Hans , so hush hush to the following or those Filmotech guys will overhear us-

Please don't say things like ....."and it is a very inexpensive film". If they now put the price up we will know who to blame. Anyway it is inevitable that these introductory pack prices are just to hook future customers. 

It will all boil down to what the competition do I guess. 

Jeff

I don't know if they have changed the base of the film. Last summer I tried three year old HF55 film and also had no trouble index matching it to glass. During the winter I was unable to use new HF53 film in my cold garage. It kept wanting to curl off the plate. But since I have added a heater and isolated my garage I have had no problems index matching the same HF53 film. When it is cold it seems that the base becomes very stiff and does not want to bend easily. When it is warm, the base seems much more flexible. I noticed the same effect with the gelatin only GF40 film.

Index matching a semi-rigid plastic like polycarbonate (again, the 0.75mm Makrofol film/plate, I previously mentioned in the context of the molding/casting coating method, is outstanding) on top of the holographic film may help a lot counter the curling tendency of the film. With such „sandwich“ assemblies I was able to make H2-exposures up to 12 minutes (for PFG-03 film).

> **Hans:** I was just looking across the Filmotec web site and noticed their recommended processing regime for the high res HF53:http://www.filmotec.de/English_Site/Pro ... -HF53e.pdfThe procedure is:- non hardening developer- Dichromate bleach- Rinse-Fix- Rinse- IPA- Immediate drying.I guess this is SHSG. Has anyone tried this recommended formula?

Not exactly the processing scheme they recommand in that pdf file but similar ones – though not with filmotec materials.

As for their bleach formula, I assume that once those A + B solutions have been mixed, it won't remain stable for a long time.

I may soon post a new formula for a rehalogenating dichromate bleach that provides far better stability (no bromine or chlorine formation) and has good keeping properties.

And regarding their fixing solution, I'd suspect it's too aggressive. Since they're getting silver chloride from the above bleach, there's actually no need for that quantity of thiosulfate (actually, sulfite alone might do the job of fixing a silver chloride emulsion). I guess one might easily dilute it to 4:1 or even 5:1.
